title: The Story Is Not Always Yours to Write
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using Serena Williams's return to professional tennis at 44 as its central case, this Admired Leadership piece examines the impulse leaders have to control and author their own narrative — and the wisdom required to recognize when the story has moved past the moment where that control is possible or desirable. Serena's return generated immediate theorizing from observers: she's chasing a title, protecting her legacy, risking it, missing the spotlight. The piece argues that what made the return remarkable was not its outcome but Serena's apparent equanimity about yielding authorship of the conclusion — her willingness to act without being able to control how the story would be received or remembered. The leadership implication is precise: the most effective leaders understand that there are moments when the institutional story, the team's story, or a situation's trajectory is no longer theirs to write. Trying to script the ending at those moments produces rigidity, defensiveness, and missed adaptations. The piece identifies two failure modes — leaders who surrender authorship too early (abdication) and those who cling to it past the point of relevance (control) — and argues the skill is in recognizing which moment you're in.
points: The most effective leaders know when the story has moved beyond their authorship: trying to script a conclusion at that moment produces rigidity and defensiveness, while the willingness to act without controlling the ending enables the adaptability that the situation actually requires.

Serena's return illustrates equanimity about narrative outcome: she walked back onto courts where 20-year-olds now compete, knowing the verdicts would be harsh and beyond her control — and acted anyway, modeling the distinction between caring about what you do and needing to control how it's interpreted.

Two failure modes bracket the leadership skill: abdication (surrendering authorship of the story before the moment has actually passed, which looks like excessive passivity) and control (clinging to narrative authorship past the point where the situation responds to it, which looks like rigidity and self-protection).

The recognition question — 'whose story is this to write now?' — is the most practically important one: it requires setting aside ego investment in the outcome and reading the actual situation, which leaders who are most personally invested in their own narrative find hardest to do accurately.

The piece's leadership application extends beyond public figures: any leader navigating succession, a team transition, an institutional pivot, or a decision whose consequences they won't fully see should ask whether their current instinct to control the story is serving the situation or only their own comfort.
quotes: When Serena Williams announced she was returning to competitive tennis after nearly four years away, everyone had a theory. At 44, walking back onto courts where 20-year-olds now roam, Serena knew the verdicts would come from every direction.

Asked about the fanfare surrounding her return, she offered one of the most instructive answers of her career: It’s not up to her what others make of it. So she stated her reasons plainly — she wanted her daughters to see her play.

This week, Serena walked off Centre Court to a standing ovation, having taken a set from a player half her age, her daughters cheering from the front row. The loss on the scoreboard didn’t touch the win she came for.

Many leaders, especially those with high global or local visibility, operate differently. They exhaust themselves managing perception, pre-spinning decisions, over-explaining, chasing down every critic.
They delay hard calls while imagining how the announcement will land. All that energy spent on the narrative is energy not spent on the work.

People judge leaders by what they repeatedly do, not by what they say about what they do. Good leaders define what they do with clear reasons, state them once, and let their consistency do the explaining.
When misunderstood, they check whether their behavior needs to change. They spend their energy where it compounds: on standards, on preparation, on the people in front of them.
